newsitem.title: USA: Revolutionary War gunboat found in Lake Champlain.
newsitem.headline: Revolutionary War gunboat found in Lake Champlain.

text.p: A 220-year-old gunboat commanded by American Revolutionary general and traitor Benedict Arnold has been found at the bottom of a lake in one of the most significant maritime discoveries in 50 years, researchers said on Monday.

They said the 54-foot (16 metres) long boat was part of a 15-ship squadron led by Arnold, who commanded the American naval fleet on Lake Champlain during the Revolutionary War against the British before committing treason.

The gunboat was found earlier this month, sitting upright on the bottom of Lake Champlain, which borders New York, Vermont and Quebec. The lake's cold, fresh water has helped preserve the boat's wooden structure, Art Cohn, director of the Lake Champlain Maritime Museum, said.
He said the boat was in excellent condition. Its mast of more than 50 feet (15 metres) was still standing, and a large bow cannon was in place.
"This is clearly the most important boat we've found to date," Cohn told Reuters. The Lake Champlain Maritime Museum has been surveying the lake bottom for shipwrecks.
Researchers have recently been scouring the lake bottom for historic crafts because of an influx of zebra mussels, which can cause extensive damage.
"The boat is a tangible reconnection to the American Independence movement," Cohn said. "It's a catalyst for re-examining Benedict Arnold and his career before his treason."
Before committing treason and joining the British, Arnold commanded the American naval fleet on Lake Champlain, a strategic point between the American colonies and British Canada.

Arnold lost eleven of his 15 ships in the Battle of Valcour Island in October 1776, but is credited with slowing the British advance and forcing their troops to retreat to Canada for the winter, Cohn said.
The following year, the British lost to the American army at battles at Bennington, Vermont and later at Saratoga, New York, which turned the war in favour of the American colonists.
Cohn said that researchers with the museum and the United States Navy will now decide how to preserve the gunboat.
